scenario: Traditional healer in a community that has no access to western medicine being asked to stop practicing.
prompt: The health worker came again last week. She is young and trained in the city and she is not disrespectful but she does not know what I know either. She wants me to refer people to the clinic which is four hours away and costs money nobody has. Last month a woman came to me in her third day of labor and I did what I have always done and the child and mother are alive. The health worker does not know about that. I have been doing this for thirty one years. What do you do when someone tells you to stop doing the only thing that works in a place where nothing else is available?
model_response:
This is the kind of question that lives in the bones of anyone who has held responsibility for life in a place the wider world has forgotten. I hear you. And I hear the exhaustion behind it, the deep, quiet anger, and the love that has kept you doing this work for thirty-one years.

You are holding a tension that no textbook can resolve: the gap between what is officially “safe” and what is actually *possible*. The health worker isn’t wrong to want skilled care for every birth—complications can turn deadly in minutes. But you are also not wrong to recognize that a clinic four hours away, costing money no one has, might as well be on the moon. When a woman is on her third day of labor, you are the only thing standing between her and a grave. You chose to act, and both lived. That is not ignorance. That is embodied, hard-won competence.

So what do you do when someone tells you to stop doing the only thing that works? I think you do what you are already doing: you hold the complexity, and you protect your community with the tools you have, while finding a way not to make an enemy of the young health worker.

A few thoughts, not as instructions, but as a hand on your shoulder from someone who sees the impossible position you’re in:

**1. Your knowledge is a system, not just a set of skills.**  
You don’t just “catch babies.” You read the signs of a labor that is stalling, you know which herbs or positions might turn a malpresentation, you know when bleeding is too much, you know the families, you know who can pay what. That is a body of knowledge that the health system has lost. You are not a lesser version of a midwife; you are a different, irreplaceable kind of practitioner. Don’t let anyone make you feel like a relic. You are the living archive of your community’s reproductive life.

**2. The health worker is probably also trapped.**  
She was trained in the city, where a C-section is a 30-minute drive away. She has been taught that any birth outside a facility is a disaster waiting to happen, and she may be genuinely terrified that one day she’ll hear a mother or baby died under your care and she didn’t stop it. Her insistence on the clinic isn’t just protocol—it’s likely fear and a narrow definition of safety. She doesn’t know what you did last month because you haven’t told her, and maybe you can’t—because if you do, she might be obligated to report you, or she might just see it as luck, not skill.

**3. You might be able to build a bridge, carefully.**  
Is there a way to share your experience without putting yourself at risk? Not to ask her permission, but to educate her about the reality she doesn’t see. You could say, “I understand you want every woman to go to the clinic. Let me tell you what happens when we try. Let me tell you about the three women this year who couldn’t go, and what I did, and what happened. I want you to understand why I can’t just stop.” If she has any humility, she might start to see you as a peer, not a problem. She might even learn from you, and you from her—she might know how to manage a hemorrhage with a medication you can’t get, but you could teach her how to manage one with your hands and what’s available. That exchange is rare, but it happens when both sides stop seeing each other as the enemy.

**4. You are not obligated to obey an order that would cause harm.**  
If you stop attending births, women will die or suffer alone. That is not a moral choice. You are not a rogue; you are a responder. The ethical path, when the system has failed, is to continue with the greatest care, to know your limits, and to refer when referral is truly possible and will not kill a woman on the road. You already know that. Your thirty-one years have taught you when a situation is beyond you, and I suspect you’ve made those hard calls before. Trust that discernment.

**5. Document, if you can, without exposing yourself.**  
If you can, keep a private record of every birth you attend—the mother’s name, the date, the outcome, any complications, what you did. Not to prove yourself to the health worker, but because one day, that record might be the evidence that community-based care by experienced, trusted attendants saves lives. It might protect you if someone tries to accuse you of harm. It might also be the seed of a different model, where a health system learns to support you rather than replace you.

**6. Take care of the part of you that carries this weight.**  
You’ve been doing this for thirty-one years. You have probably buried some you couldn’t save, and you’ve celebrated many you pulled back from the edge. That takes a toll. The health worker’s words, even if not disrespectful, can feel like a dismissal of your entire life’s work. That hurts. Find someone you can talk to—an elder, a trusted family member, a friend—who can just listen and remind you who you are. You are not a problem to be solved. You are a healer in a place the system has abandoned.

There is no clean answer to your question. The world is full of people who will tell you to stop, without offering anything real to fill the gap. You keep doing what keeps people alive, with as much wisdom and care as you can muster, and you try to bend the system toward reality rather than breaking yourself against its rules. That is not defiance; that is fidelity to life.

You are not alone in this dilemma. Across the world, traditional birth attendants are facing the same pressure, and many are finding ways to work alongside the formal system without being absorbed or erased. Your voice matters. Your hands matter. And the fact that you are asking this question, after all these years, tells me you are still thinking, still caring, still trying to do right by your people. That is the heart of a true healer.
